rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate the eight peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting late elution. The intermediate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Test a substantial temperature change at the same gradient to probe selectivity within the crowded middle group and final pair. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving room for later gradient expansion.

Use a substantially shallower gradient at the better-performing temperature to spread the crowded groups and test slope-dependent selectivity. The short current elution window provides room to improve resolution without a time penalty.

The shallower gradient resolved the middle cluster but left one near-coelution. Lower temperature by one step to shift that pair’s selectivity while retaining the successful gradient and likely keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction while keeping the endpoint and duration fixed, producing a shallower gradient with earlier elution. This tests whether the remaining critical pair can gain resolution without pushing the last peak beyond 10 minutes.

At 60 C, an intermediate gradient duration may separate the late pair that nearly coeluted at 24 minutes while preserving enough resolution in the middle cluster. This also keeps the final peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

This gives a slightly steeper slope (0.045 versus 0.0444 organic fraction per minute) than injection 6, targeting the lone R=1.49 pair while preserving the middle pairs. The endpoint remains above the organic fraction reached when the last peak eluted in injection 6.
Injection 7 reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test whether full resolution can be retained with faster elution.

The two-minute shortening was too aggressive, so retain injection 7 as the best method and test a finer slope increase from 0.045 to 0.04583 per minute. This should slightly accelerate elution while probing the narrow full-resolution boundary.

The full-resolution slope window at phi0=0.10 is narrow, so test a higher starting fraction with a gentler slope of 0.040 per minute. This may shorten retention while compensating for the middle-cluster compression caused by starting at higher organic strength.

Make the gradient one step shallower to improve the remaining R=1.08 pair at the higher starting organic fraction. The other pairs have some margin, and the final peak may still elute sooner than in injection 7.

Injection 7 already achieves the maximum score; the higher-starting-organic branch has not improved it. Test the low-temperature selectivity regime with a moderate gradient to look for a different, potentially faster fully resolved separation.
Test whether a steeper gradient moves the low-temperature near-coelution apart while shortening the run. This isolates slope effects at 25 C; injection 7 remains the fully resolved benchmark.

Increase temperature by one step to test whether selectivity can resolve the two remaining low-temperature critical pairs without lengthening the gradient. Injection 7 remains the maximum-score fallback.

At low temperature, steepening the gradient improved the middle near-coelution; test a larger slope increase at 30 C, where the late pair has resolution margin. This probes a faster separation while retaining injection 7 as the proven maximum-score method.

Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving injection 14’s gradient slope to test a different selectivity adjustment for its lone critical pair. This avoids the strong compression seen with the six-minute gradient and may yield a faster fully resolved alternative to injection 7.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a gentler slope to redistribute and expand the middle cluster while keeping retention short. Injection 7 remains the proven maximum-score method if this alternative does not fully resolve the mixture.

Lower temperature one step to improve the remaining middle-cluster separation; earlier runs suggest cooling benefits this region. The late pair currently has enough resolution margin to make this a promising test of a much faster fully resolved method.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to lift the late pair from R=1.43 toward baseline resolution, using the modest resolution margin in the middle cluster. This refines the promising four-minute separation while retaining injection 7 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Injection 19 matches the maximum CRF with much earlier elution. Test a higher starting fraction and temperature for further speed, offset by a shallower gradient to protect the middle-cluster resolution.

Lower temperature one step while holding the gradient fixed to improve the lone unresolved middle pair, as cooling did between injections 17 and 18. The late-pair margin may accommodate this change and yield full resolution sooner than injection 19.
Injection 21 is now the fastest fully resolved method. Shorten its gradient by one grid step to test the speed limit, retaining injection 21 if either critical pair drops below R=1.5.

The steeper gradient lost resolution, so test a higher starting organic fraction paired with a shallower slope to shorten retention while restoring separation of the critical middle pair. Injection 21 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.

Return to the fastest fully resolved starting fraction and test a smaller slope increase than injection 22. This brackets the speed–resolution boundary near injection 21, which remains the preferred proven method.

Preserve injection 21’s successful slope of 0.050 per minute while ending the programmed gradient earlier. The gradient endpoint reaches the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after the previous last peak at 4.14 minutes, so this should retain full resolution and CRF 1.000 with a shorter programmed gradient.
